how-much-to-charge-to-refinish-hardwood-.text:
← Hardwood refinishing bid calculator

How much to charge to refinish hardwood floors

The number a homeowner wants is a price per square foot. That number is not a takeoff. A 400 sq ft living room of screen-and-recoat is not the same job as 400 sq ft of hallway plus fourteen stair treads, two closets, and a stain change. The footage is identical. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count stair treads and closets, not just room footage

A typical first floor has a stair run the homeowner never includes in the living-room number, and every closet still has to be cut in. Flooring install prices waste and tear-out. Hardwood refinishing prices sanding time on surfaces that do not show up in a tape-measure of the field. Quoting both from a published per-square-foot number is how the stairs eat the field margin.

Screen-and-recoat and full sand are different jobs

Buffing an existing finish and rolling two coats is the fastest refinish. Full sand — cut-in around the edges, field passes, a sealer, and two finish coats — is a different crew-day. The calculator keeps a hours-per-100 figure on the field only. Stairs, closets, furniture, and repairs stay their own hours so a dustless adder cannot hide which part of a high bid is sanding time.

Stain follows the finish area, including treads

Stain and a color-change extra coat are labor on every sanded square foot, including treads and risers. A 14-tread hallway can put more than fifteen percent of the job’s hours on stairs the homeowner never counted. Treating that as a blended “add 20%” is how the hallway special that looked fine turns into a loss.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $42/h finisher loaded at 30% payroll burden is $54.60. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. On the sample 800 sq ft first floor with 12 treads the calculator prices about $7,604 ($9.50 per field square foot, 75.3 crew-hours, walk-away $5,703). The same house as sand-and-stain is several hundred dollars more. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a flooring specification, an adhesion or sheen warranty, a permit, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Grit sequence, dustless containment, and whether stairs are stained to match are yours to confirm.

Price your floor

Common questions

How much to charge to refinish hardwood floors?

Charge from field square footage, stair treads, closets, screen-and-recoat versus full sand, stain, extra coats for a color change, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 800 sq ft first floor with 12 treads on full sand prices around $7,604 on the sample rates in this calculator — about $9.50 per field square foot.

Why is a per-square-foot hardwood quote dangerous?

Homeowners measure rooms. Stair treads, closets, stain, and an extra coat do not scale with that footage. Matching a cheaper per-square-foot quote written for a same-color screen-and-recoat is how a sand-and-stain hallway with a stair run becomes a loss.

How much extra should I charge for stairs when refinishing hardwood?

Treat each tread as its own hours plus a few square feet of tread and riser for finish gallons — not a blended add-on to the living-room footage. On the sample rates that is about 0.4 hours per tread. A 14-tread hallway can put more than 15% of the job's hours on stairs the homeowner never counted.

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not flooring, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

FOR HARDWOOD FLOOR REFINISHERS

Bid the stairs, the closets, and the stain — not the square footage.

A flat per-square-foot quote treats a 400 sq ft living room of screen-and-recoat as the same job as 400 sq ft of hallway plus fourteen stair treads, two closets, and a stain change. Stairs, closets, and extra coats do not scale with the room footage the homeowner measures. Price those extras separately, then see the walk-away number.

The floor

Start from a common job, then replace every rate with numbers from your own crew and invoices. Picking a method or stain fills hours-per-100, coats, and extra coats only if you have not already changed them.

Your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation, liability insurance, and paid time off. A $42/h finisher loaded at 30% is $54.60. Quoting the raw wage is how a per-square-foot special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first stair run.

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and coverage are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a flooring specification — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      Why is a 250 sq ft hallway with 14 treads a losing job at a per-square-foot rate?

      Because stair treads are billed at their own hours per tread, not folded into the field square footage — each tread is estimated at about 4 sq ft of tread-and-riser for the finish and stain math, but its labor is a separate line entirely. A small hallway with a lot of stairs can carry more total labor hours than a much larger open room with none, which a flat rate written for the room square footage cannot see.

      Why does full sand cost so much more than screen and recoat on the same floor?

      Screen and recoat starts at 3.5 hours per 100 sq ft with 2 base coats; full sand — cutting in and sanding the field down to bare wood — starts at 8 hours per 100 sq ft with 3 base coats. Both the labor rate and the coat count are higher, so the gap between the two methods compounds rather than adding once, which matters most on a same-color job where the temptation is to assume the cheaper method looks the same when it’s done.

      Why does a stain color change add a whole extra coat, not just stain time?

      A poly-only job needs no stain step at all. Stain-then-finish adds stain application time across the full finish area, but a color change adds an additional finish coat on top of that — because covering an existing color evenly typically takes one more pass than staining bare wood. That extra coat’s hours and gallons are counted separately from the base coats the method itself sets.

      Why does the gallon count round up instead of matching the math exactly?

      Because you can’t buy a fraction of a gallon of finish or stain. Gallons needed is finish area times coat count divided by coverage per gallon, then rounded up to the next whole gallon — so a job that calculates to 4.05 gallons still buys 5, and that rounding happens independently for the clear finish and for the stain, since they don’t share a coverage rate.

      Do closets and furniture moving get folded into the field square footage?

      No — each closet adds its own fixed hours per closet regardless of its size, and furniture-move and repair hours are flat inputs on top of everything else, none of which scale with floor square footage. A job with several small closets and a furniture-heavy room can carry meaningfully more labor than the field square footage alone would suggest.

      What does “Copy share link” send, and does anything leave my browser?

      It copies the current page’s address with the field square footage, stair and closet counts, method, stain choice, coats, and every rate encoded after a # in the URL. A browser never sends the part after # to a server, so pasting that link into a text or email is the only way the figures travel — opening it re-runs the same bid immediately, so a partner, estimator, or customer sees the exact job you priced rather than a screenshot of the total. Your business name, licence, and the customer’s name and address are never included; those stay on this device.

A share link encodes only the bid fields above in the page’s URL hash — it is not sent to us, and it never includes your business or customer details.

vs-a-flat-price-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Hardwood Refinishing Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per square foot

“$X a square foot” is not a price for a hardwood refinish — it is a price for one specific method, floor plan, and finish, quietly applied to every room that calls in.

What a flat price per square foot is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote a refinishing job: multiply the field footage by a number and read off a price. It is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer or a search-result special will call and ask you to match, whatever their floor actually needs.

The number behind it was set for one job — a living room of same-color screen-and-recoat, no stairs, no closets, no stain change — and then reused for every refinish afterward, whether or not the next job looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the field square footage, stair treads, closets, the refinishing method (screen-and-recoat or full sand), whether the job is staining or a color change, and your own labor hours and material costs. It prices the treads, the closets, and the stain separately by kind, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this floor, not a generic one.

What a flat price per square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sq ft whether the room has zero stair treads or fourteen, even though every tread adds its own hours plus tread-and-riser finish area the field footage never counts. Prices stair treads separately as their own hours and their own finish area, so a stair-heavy job costs more than a flat field of the same size.
Has no line for a stain color change or the extra coat it needs, regardless of whether the job is poly-only or a full color change. Prices stain and extra-coat hours and gallons separately, following the finish area including treads, so a color change costs more than a poly-only recoat.
Charges the same rate for a full sand as for a screen-and-recoat, even though a full sand runs several times the hours per 100 sq ft. Prices each method's own hours-per-100 figure, so a full sand costs more than a screen-and-recoat of the same field.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against a flat per-square-foot rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two floors, the same field-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($42/hr crew wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, a 25% target margin):

250 sq ft hallway, full sand, 14 stair treads, stain color change — the “stairs trap” preset, 306 sq ft of actual finish area once the treads are counted$3,599.92 bid price; $2,699.94 break-even cost$1,272.57The rate quotes $1,427.37 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $2,327.35 below the calculator's own bid price.

The $5.09/sq ft rate is not invented — it is this calculator's own price on the screen-and-recoat living-room preset, divided by that preset's field square footage. It fits that one job by construction. Applied to the stair-heavy, stained hallway, it prices only the 250 sq ft of field and never sees the fourteen treads or the stain change at all. Run your own room's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat per-square-foot rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one floor it was built for, and nothing about a flat number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per square foot get a hardwood refinishing bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is stair treads, closets, method (screen-and-recoat versus full sand), a stain color change, and extra coats — not the field square footage a homeowner measures. A 250 sq ft hallway with fourteen stair treads and a stain change is doing far more work than a 250 sq ft living room of same-color screen-and-recoat, none of which shows up in the room's own square footage.

What does a flat price per square foot usually leave out entirely?

Stair treads and their extra tread-and-riser finish area, closets, whether the job is a full sand or a screen-and-recoat, a stain color change, and any extra coat that change requires. A hallway with fourteen treads is doing several times the labor of the same field square footage with no stairs at all, and a per-square-foot number has no line for any of it.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates: a 400 sq ft living room of screen-and-recoat prices at $2,036.11, or $5.09 a field square foot. Applying that same $5.09 rate to a 250 sq ft hallway with fourteen stair treads and a stain color change — 306 sq ft of actual finish area once the treads are counted — quotes $1,272.57, which is $1,427.37 below that job's own $2,699.94 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $2,327.35 below the calculator's own $3,599.92 bid price.

Is a flat price per square foot ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs — same method, no stairs, no closets, no stain change — a per-square-foot rate can land close, and on this calculator's own screen-and-recoat living-room preset it is exactly the rate that job supports, because it was set from that job. The risk is applying the same rate outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which floor it was built on and neither does the estimator until stairs, closets, method, and stain are actually spelled out.

Does this calculator know what materials or labor cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates. It takes the field square footage, stair treads, closets, method, stain, and coats, plus the labor hours, finish and stain costs, and wage you enter, and turns that into a price for this job — the arithmetic a flat per-square-foot rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number on this page and in the calculator stays on this device; this page names no company, product, or service, so it makes no claim about how anyone else prices a job.

← Hardwood Refinishing Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is an account-based platform for running a home service company's whole operation, including scheduling the crew and invoicing the customer once a job is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this hardwood refinish cost, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is a field service management platform used by home service businesses — flooring, cleaning, HVAC, plumbing, and lawn care among them — to run client management and online quoting, scheduling and crew dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client-facing hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. Jobber's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of field service software describe scheduling, invoicing, and collecting payment for a job once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a hardwood refinish should cost from field square footage, stair treads, and closets before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage a client list, dispatch a route across a season, or collect a payment. It takes field square footage, stair treads, closets, a stain change, and extra coats as their own line items, plus loaded refinisher wage, payroll burden, travel, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the price, the price per square foot, the share of hours eaten by stairs, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
